title: Carryover ladder
purpose: Carry the voice you like from simple, automatic speech into longer and more spontaneous speech, one step at a time.
instructions: Start with short, simple, automatic speech, so you can focus on how you say it rather than what you say.
Use your practised voice for the current step.
Only move up a step when you can produce your voice comfortably and consistently.
If a step feels too hard, step back and spend more time on the previous one.

primary_cue.text: Keep your practised voice for the whole step, comfortably.

cues.text: Keep your practised voice for the whole step, comfortably.
Step back to the previous step and give it more time.

practice_task.prompt_text: Use your practised voice for the current ladder step.

ladder.text: Say the months of the year.
Say your name, address and phone number (record it privately, or use made-up details).
Read a few short sentences from a news website.
Talk aloud for one minute on any topic you like.
Say short phrases you use in real life, like getting on the bus, answering the phone, or greeting someone.
Read several paragraphs from a book aloud.
Have a short conversation with someone you know well.

check_questions.text: Could you keep your practised voice comfortably through this step?

dose_guidance.text: The source suggests short, frequent practice through the day, for example 3–4 minutes around 8–10 times a day, to build muscle memory and reduce voice fatigue. It sets no time per step. Lilt only records what you choose to log.

progression_rule.text: Lilt offers the next step after two sessions in a row where you report “comfortably and consistently” at the current step.
progression_rule.source_basis: The source says to increase difficulty only when you can produce your voice comfortably and consistently. It gives no count; two sessions is Lilt's own setting.

expected_observations: It is not usually a steady process. Some steps take longer than others.
common_misunderstandings: Doing well in reading does not show how your voice works in everyday conversation.
Moving up faster is not better.
stop_conditions: Stop the activity if you feel pain or discomfort, or notice unintended voice changes such as hoarseness. The source says this may mean you are going too quickly.
Take time to look after your voice, and try again when it feels better.
If problems persist or keep coming back, seek advice from a voice professional such as a speech and language therapist.
Respond to any pain or discomfort by stopping and taking a step back.
adaptations: Build your own order of speech situations that works for you.
limitations: Public NHS patient-advice material written for self-guided practice. Lilt cannot check your technique, and it does not replace a speech and language therapist.
The last two steps happen away from Lilt. Lilt records only what you report about them.
